narrative:
The model predicted a 98% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to decide on offers, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily against you were your class ranking in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average ranking of students who were accepted. This was the single largest reason the model expected you to struggle with the bar. Your LSAT score of 25 was also well below the 37-point average of accepted students and added substantial additional risk in the model’s eyes. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants, further reinforced the outlook.

Your undergraduate GPA of 1.8, also much lower than the 3.23 average of admitted students, added to the concern, though it was not among the top three drivers. Your family income, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time did not influence the decision; the model ignored those characteristics.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance if you retake any courses, consider retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s, and look for post-graduation bar-preparation programs that target students with similar profiles. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (248 words)
